Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- North Korea accused the United States and South Korea of sending spy planes on about 200 missions near the isolated communist nation ahead of a North Korea rocket launch scheduled for early April. Pyongyang claims reconnaissance aircraft, including the high-altitude U-2 spy plane, have flown spy missions. "The U.S. imperialists and the South Korean puppet military warmongers perpetrated intensive aerial espionage against the DPRK (North Korea) in March by massively mobilizing strategic and tactical reconnaissance planes with various missions," a military source said, according to a report from North Korea's state-run news service, KCNA, on Tuesday. Pyongyang said the United States committed 110 cases of "aerial espionage and the South Korean puppet forces at least 80 cases," during March, KCNA reported. The source said the missions utilized six types of reconnaissance aircraft, including the high-altitude U-2 spy plane. "The U.S. imperialist warmongers had better bear in mind that ... spy planes perpetrating espionage against the DPRK are within the range of its strikes." The Pentagon was not immediately available to comment on the story. The North Korean government says it will launch a commercial satellite atop a rocket sometime between April 4 and April 8. Satellite imagery taken on Sunday appears to show a rocket at the Musudan-ri launch site in northeastern North Korea. U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates said Sunday there is little doubt that the planned rocket launch is designed to bolster North Korea's military capability. He also indicated that the U.S. military could be prepared to shoot down a North Korean missile if the rogue regime develops the capability to reach Hawaii or the western continental United States in a future launch.  Watch analysis of Pyongyang's planned rocket launch » . Both the United States and Japan have mobilized missile defense systems ahead of the launch. North Korea has threatened to start a war if Japan were to shoot down its rocket. Tokyo said the move is aimed at shooting down any debris from the launch that might fall into Japanese territory. U.S. Navy ships capable of shooting down ballistic missiles have been moved to the Sea of Japan, a Navy spokesman said. The United States generally has a number of ships equipped with powerful Aegis radar in the Sea of Japan because of North Korean threats to launch rockets. The ships are designed to track and, if needed, shoot down ballistic missiles. The United States has no plans to shoot down the North Korean rocket, U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton said last week, but will raise the issue with the U.N. Security Council if Pyongyang carries out a launch.

outputs.L1:
(CNN) — North Korea has accused the United States and South Korea of conducting approximately 200 spy-plane missions near the isolated communist nation ahead of a North Korean rocket launch scheduled for early April.

Pyongyang claims that reconnaissance aircraft, including the high-altitude U-2 spy plane, have carried out espionage missions.

“The U.S. imperialists and the South Korean puppet military warmongers perpetrated intensive aerial espionage against the DPRK (North Korea) in March by massively mobilizing strategic and tactical reconnaissance planes with various missions,” a military source said Tuesday, according to North Korea’s state-run news service, KCNA.

Pyongyang said the United States conducted 110 cases of “aerial espionage,” while “the South Korean puppet forces” carried out at least 80 cases during March, KCNA reported.

The source said the missions involved six types of reconnaissance aircraft, including the high-altitude U-2 spy plane.

“The U.S. imperialist warmongers had better bear in mind that ... spy planes perpetrating espionage against the DPRK are within the range of its strikes.”

The Pentagon was not immediately available for comment.

The North Korean government says it will launch a commercial satellite aboard a rocket sometime between April 4 and April 8. Satellite imagery taken Sunday appears to show a rocket at the Musudan-ri launch site in northeastern North Korea.

U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates said Sunday that there is little doubt the planned rocket launch is intended to strengthen North Korea’s military capability. He also indicated that the U.S. military could be prepared to shoot down a North Korean missile if the rogue regime develops the capability, in a future launch, to reach Hawaii or the western continental United States.

Watch analysis of Pyongyang’s planned rocket launch »

Both the United States and Japan have mobilized missile-defense systems ahead of the launch. North Korea has threatened to start a war if Japan shoots down its rocket. Tokyo said its preparations are intended to intercept any debris from the launch that might fall on Japanese territory.

U.S. Navy ships capable of intercepting ballistic missiles have been deployed to the Sea of Japan, a Navy spokesman said. Because of North Korean threats to launch rockets, the United States generally maintains several ships equipped with powerful Aegis radar systems in the area. The ships are designed to track and, if necessary, shoot down ballistic missiles.

The United States has no plans to shoot down the North Korean rocket, U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton said last week. However, she said Washington would raise the issue with the U.N. Security Council if Pyongyang proceeds with the launch.
outputs.L2:
(CNN) — North Korea alleged that U.S. and South Korean reconnaissance aircraft carried out roughly 200 flights near the isolated communist country in March, shortly before Pyongyang’s planned rocket launch in early April.

According to a Tuesday report by North Korea’s state-controlled Korean Central News Agency (KCNA), Pyongyang said several kinds of surveillance aircraft—including the high-altitude U-2—were used in the operations. A military source quoted by KCNA accused what it called U.S. “imperialists” and South Korean “puppet military warmongers” of conducting an intense aerial spying campaign against the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea by deploying numerous strategic and tactical reconnaissance planes for different assignments.

KCNA reported that North Korea attributed 110 alleged espionage flights to the United States and at least 80 to South Korean forces during March. The military source said six models of reconnaissance aircraft took part and warned that planes spying on North Korea were within range of the country’s weapons.

The Pentagon could not immediately be reached for a response.

Pyongyang says it intends to place a commercial satellite into orbit using a rocket scheduled for launch sometime from April 4 through April 8. Satellite photographs captured Sunday appear to show a rocket positioned at the Musudan-ri launch facility in northeastern North Korea.

On Sunday, U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates said there was little question that the launch was intended to strengthen North Korea’s military capabilities. He also suggested that the U.S. military might be ready to intercept a North Korean missile during a future launch if the regime acquires the ability to reach Hawaii or the western mainland United States.

In preparation for the planned launch, both Japan and the United States have deployed missile-defense equipment. North Korea has warned that it would initiate a war if Japan attempted to destroy the rocket. Tokyo, however, said its preparations were meant to intercept any launch debris that could land on Japanese territory.

A U.S. Navy spokesman said American warships with the ability to destroy ballistic missiles had been sent to the Sea of Japan. Because of North Korean rocket-launch threats, the United States ordinarily keeps several vessels fitted with powerful Aegis radar systems in the area. Those ships can monitor ballistic missiles and shoot them down if necessary.

U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton said the previous week that Washington did not intend to intercept North Korea’s rocket. She added, however, that the United States would bring the matter before the U.N. Security Council if Pyongyang proceeded with the launch.

CNN has long reported on North Korea, one of the world’s most isolated countries. Its coverage often focuses on the government’s nuclear and missile programs, relations with South Korea and the United States, and the impact of international sanctions.

counterfactuals.output:
**North Korea alleges surge in US, South Korean spy flights ahead of rocket launch**

**SEOUL, South Korea** — North Korea has accused the United States and South Korea of conducting roughly 200 aerial espionage missions near its territory as Pyongyang prepares for a controversial rocket launch in April.

The allegation, carried by North Korean state media, claimed US and South Korean reconnaissance aircraft repeatedly monitored strategic sites during the previous month. Pyongyang characterized the flights as evidence that the allies were increasing military pressure ahead of the launch.

Neither Washington nor Seoul immediately confirmed the number of missions cited by North Korea. The United States and South Korea routinely conduct surveillance of the heavily militarized peninsula, particularly during periods of heightened tension.

North Korea has said it plans to send a communications satellite into orbit aboard a rocket during an announced launch window in early April. The United States, South Korea and Japan say the launch could serve as a test of long-range ballistic missile technology and may violate United Nations restrictions.

Pyongyang insists the program is peaceful and has warned against any attempt to intercept the rocket. Regional governments have stepped up monitoring, while Japan has said it could act if debris threatens its territory.

The accusations come amid broader tensions over North Korea’s nuclear and missile programs. Analysts say heightened reconnaissance would not be unusual before a launch, but North Korea frequently portrays allied surveillance and military exercises as preparations for an attack.

The planned launch has prompted calls for restraint and renewed diplomatic efforts to prevent the situation from escalating.

It said U.S. forces routinely conduct lawful reconnaissance in international airspace and were closely monitoring North Korea’s announced launch. Washington, Seoul and Tokyo believed the launch—scheduled for April 4–8, 2009—would test long-range Taepodong-2 missile technology, although Pyongyang said it would place a communications satellite into orbit.

**BREAKING: North Korea accuses U.S., South Korea of spying, warns aircraft are within missile range**

**SEOUL —** North Korea has accused the United States and South Korea of intensifying aerial surveillance around the Korean Peninsula, warning that reconnaissance aircraft operating near its territory are “within striking range,” according to statements carried by state media.

Pyongyang alleged that U.S. and South Korean aircraft had conducted repeated intelligence flights near its airspace. It did not provide independently verifiable evidence that the aircraft entered North Korean territory.

The warning raised concerns about a potential confrontation in one of the world’s most heavily militarized regions. North Korea has previously threatened to shoot down U.S. reconnaissance planes it says violate its airspace, while Washington maintains that its surveillance missions are conducted in accordance with international law.

North Korea also criticized Japan’s expanding military cooperation with the United States, including preparations involving U.S. missile-defense ships. American Aegis-equipped destroyers regularly operate in the region to track and potentially intercept ballistic missiles, a capability Washington and its allies describe as defensive.

Pyongyang portrays the deployment of missile-defense systems and U.S.-Japan-South Korea security cooperation as preparations for war. The three countries say their coordination is a response to North Korea’s nuclear weapons program and repeated ballistic-missile launches.

There was no immediate independent confirmation of North Korea’s claims or public indication that a reconnaissance aircraft had been targeted. U.S., South Korean and Japanese officials have repeatedly urged Pyongyang to avoid actions that could lead to miscalculation, while pledging to maintain surveillance and missile-defense readiness.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the controversy surrounding North Korea’s planned April 4–8 satellite launch, incorporating KCNA’s espionage accusations, Robert Gates’s comments, and Hillary Clinton’s stated U.S. policy.
counterfactuals.output:
North Korea said it would launch a communications satellite between April 4 and 8, but the United States, Japan, and South Korea viewed the launch as a disguised test of the Taepodong-2 long-range ballistic missile and a likely violation of U.N. Security Council resolutions restricting Pyongyang’s missile activity.

KCNA portrayed the mounting surveillance as hostile preparation, accusing the United States and its allies of conducting intensive aerial espionage around North Korea and warning that interference with the launch could trigger retaliation.

U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates sought to limit expectations of a military response. He said Washington did not plan to shoot the rocket down under normal circumstances, although it could act if the vehicle appeared to threaten U.S. territory, such as Hawaii. He also suggested the launch was intended to advance North Korea’s long-range missile capability despite its “satellite” label.

Secretary of State Hillary Clinton emphasized the diplomatic line: Washington regarded the launch as provocative and inconsistent with U.N. restrictions, would bring the matter before the Security Council, and would seek consequences through international pressure rather than treating interception as the default response. At the same time, the United States remained committed to the six-party process and North Korea’s denuclearization.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a detailed international news report about North Korea’s imminent Musudan-ri rocket launch, alleged surveillance flights, U.S. and Japanese missile-defense deployments, and the possibility of U.N. Security Council action.
counterfactuals.output:
**North Korea rocket launch appears imminent as regional defenses go on alert**

*SEOUL/TOKYO, April 3, 2009* — North Korea appeared close to launching a long-range rocket from its Musudan-ri facility on the country’s east coast, intensifying military surveillance across Northeast Asia and prompting the United States and Japan to deploy missile-defense assets.

Pyongyang has informed international aviation and maritime authorities that it plans to launch what it calls the **Kwangmyongsong-2 communications satellite** aboard an **Unha-2 rocket** between April 4 and April 8. South Korean, Japanese and U.S. officials, however, say the launch vehicle is closely related to the North’s Taepodong-2 ballistic missile and could provide data useful for developing a weapon capable of reaching targets far beyond the Korean Peninsula.

Officials monitoring the launch site said preparations appeared to be in their final stages, although weather and technical factors could still affect the timing. North Korea has identified danger zones in waters east of Japan and over the Pacific where the rocket’s stages are expected to fall.

The planned launch has revived concerns over North Korea’s missile and nuclear programs, less than three years after it conducted its first nuclear test and attempted to launch a Taepodong-2. That 2006 rocket failed shortly after liftoff. Analysts said even a satellite attempt would allow North Korean engineers to test propulsion, staging, guidance and other technologies relevant to an intercontinental ballistic missile.

### Surveillance claims

North Korea accused the United States, Japan and South Korea of sharply increasing aerial surveillance around the peninsula as the launch window approached. State media alleged that American reconnaissance aircraft had conducted repeated flights near North Korean airspace to monitor military facilities and the Musudan-ri site.

The claims could not be independently verified. U.S. and South Korean forces routinely conduct reconnaissance missions in the region, and military specialists said surveillance would be expected before a launch of this scale. Aircraft and naval vessels equipped to detect heat signatures, track trajectories and collect electronic data were believed to be operating in the area.

Pyongyang warned that it would regard any attempt to intercept the rocket as an act of war. It also threatened retaliation against surveillance operations that it said violated its sovereignty, though it did not provide evidence that foreign aircraft had entered North Korean airspace.

### Japan and United States deploy defenses

Japan placed its missile-defense forces on heightened alert and authorized units to destroy any rocket or debris judged likely to fall on Japanese territory.

Tokyo deployed **Aegis-equipped destroyers** carrying Standard Missile-3 interceptors to waters around Japan. It also moved **Patriot Advanced Capability-3**, or PAC-3, batteries to locations including the Tokyo area and northern Japan. The government stressed that the order was defensive and applied only if the rocket, a stage or debris threatened Japanese territory.

North Korea’s declared flight path was expected to carry the rocket over or near northern Japan. Japanese officials urged residents to remain calm, saying there was no indication that Pyongyang intended to attack Japan, but local authorities prepared emergency communication systems in case of falling debris or a failed launch.

The United States also repositioned Aegis-capable naval vessels in the region to monitor the launch and provide missile-defense coverage. Washington did not publicly commit itself to intercepting a rocket that followed the announced satellite trajectory, and senior officials indicated that the immediate priority was tracking the vehicle and protecting U.S. forces and allies.

Military analysts said interception would be technically and politically difficult unless the rocket clearly threatened populated territory. An unsuccessful attempt could expose limitations in regional missile defenses, while a successful interception of a nominal satellite launch could provoke a serious confrontation with Pyongyang.

### Dispute over legality

The United States, Japan and South Korea argue that the launch would violate **U.N. Security Council Resolution 1718**, adopted after North Korea’s 2006 nuclear test. The resolution demands that Pyongyang suspend activities related to its ballistic missile program.

North Korea maintains that it has a sovereign right to peaceful space exploration and says the planned launch is not a missile test. It has presented the mission as a scientific and technological achievement, rejecting what it calls a discriminatory attempt to deny it access to space.

The distinction is unlikely to satisfy Washington and its allies because satellite launchers and long-range ballistic missiles rely on much of the same technology. Japanese officials have said they would ask the Security Council to respond promptly if the launch proceeds.

### Security Council response uncertain

Diplomats said an emergency Security Council meeting was likely after any launch. Possible measures range from a formal statement condemning North Korea to tighter enforcement or expansion of sanctions already authorized under Resolution 1718.

Securing a strong response, however, could prove difficult. China and Russia, both permanent members with veto power, have urged restraint and called on all parties to avoid actions that could destabilize the region. They may resist new sanctions, particularly if North Korea succeeds in portraying the event as a civilian satellite launch.

Western diplomats are expected to argue that the type of payload is less important than the ballistic technology being tested. China and Russia could instead favor a nonbinding statement and renewed diplomatic talks.

A divided Council would allow Pyongyang to claim political vindication, but even a limited response could trigger retaliation. North Korea has warned that Security Council punishment would undermine the six-party negotiations aimed at ending its nuclear program. It has previously threatened to abandon agreements, restore disabled nuclear facilities or take further military steps when faced with sanctions.

### Regional stakes

The launch comes as diplomacy over North Korea’s nuclear program remains stalled. Negotiations involving the two Koreas, the United States, China, Japan and Russia have been unable to resolve disagreements over verification of Pyongyang’s nuclear declaration and the terms of further disarmament.

South Korea has urged the North to cancel the launch, warning that it would deepen isolation and increase regional tension. Seoul’s military has strengthened monitoring but has avoided suggesting that it plans to intercept the rocket.

Analysts said the launch could serve several purposes for North Korea: demonstrating technological progress, strengthening its bargaining position, reinforcing domestic propaganda and testing the approach of the U.S. administration of President Barack Obama.

Whether the rocket successfully places a satellite in orbit may matter less diplomatically than the fact that it leaves the launch pad. Once it does, attention will shift quickly from Musudan-ri to New York, where the Security Council will face pressure to decide whether the launch constitutes a prohibited missile test—and how far it is prepared to go in response.
